Chandragupta Maurya. Chandragupta Maurya (c. 340 to 293 BCE) was the founder of the Mauryan Empire, the first pan-Indian empire to unify most of the Indian subcontinent under a single rule. Rising from humble origins to overthrow the fragmented Nanda dynasty, Chandragupta established a powerful centralized state backed by a vast army and sophisticated bureaucracy. His empire laid the foundation for Indian civilization, and his grandson Ashoka became perhaps the greatest ruler in Indian history. Chandragupta was born into obscurity, possibly a member of a lower caste or merchant family; he rose through military service and political cunning. He was tutored by Kautilya (also known as Chanakya), a legendary political strategist and author of the Arthashastra, a treatise on statecraft and warfare that shaped Chandragupta's governance. Chandragupta defeated the Nanda dynasty, the rulers of the Ganges valley, establishing control of northern India around 321 BCE; this became the foundation of the Mauryan Empire. He built the largest empire India had seen to that point, controlling most of the Indian subcontinent except the southern Deccan; the empire stretched from the Arabian Sea to the Bay of Bengal. Organized the empire with a centralized bureaucracy, a vast standing army reportedly numbering 600,000, and an network of spies; the state controlled mines, agriculture, and trade to generate wealth. Made peace with the Greek Seleucid Empire (Alexander the Great's successor state in Asia), stabilizing India's northwestern frontier; this contact brought Greek culture into the Indian world. Abdicated in favor of his son Bindusara around 297 BCE and retired to a Jain monastery, reflecting the pluralistic spirituality of ancient Indian philosophy.
